utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me welcome this morning everybody in the courtroom, the Prosecution, the Defence, and the accused. Mr. Ibrisimovic, do you have any news from Mr. Pusic? We heard that he's better, but maybe his counsel knows more. We are going to move into private session before that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I read the decision, I give you the floor, registrar, to give us an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... 5D submitted a list of objections to tender through Witness CT. That will be given Exhibit number IC 217. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will read very slowly the oral decision that follows: The decision relates to additional time granted an accused during cross-examination. The Trial Chamber will fix the time for examination and cross-examination of every witness in keeping with the envisaged time by the Prosecution on the estimate of the 19th of January, 2006, in keeping with Rule 65 ter of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Trial Chamber also grants additional time to every accused depending on possible requests with regard to witnesses, either through oral testimony or exhibits that are produced by the Prosecution during examination-in-chief. Under these circumstances, the Trial Chamber set the time allowed for examination-in-chief for Witness CU at three hours, specifying that the accused would have respectively for Mr. Pusic one hour, for Mr. Praljak one hour, for all the other accused 30 minutes each. During yesterday's hearing, the counsel of Mr. Pusic indicated that he would cede one part of his time to accused Praljak. In view of that, having used 15 minutes, Mr. Pusic's counsel in theory ceded to Mr. Praljak 45 minutes. The Prosecution has objected to this manner of proceeding. The Trial Chamber has confirmed -- has conferred yesterday on this issue and decided to proceed as follows in the future: Additional time granted an accused should not be used solely except for his -- should be used solely for his own cross-examination and cannot be used by another accused. As a result, following this oral decision, Accused Praljak does not have at his disposal today more than 45 minutes having used 15 minutes yesterday. There it is. We are now going to move into private session, lower the blinds, and usher in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we're in open session, Mr. Murphy would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I will not take very long, but I did ask to go into open session for the purpose of addressing one or two issues that arose before the break, and this does not involve anything that cannot be said in open session. Your Honour, the entire Defence, I believe, is somewhat concerned by one or two of the things that the Bench mentioned just before the break in response to Mr. Praljak. Primarily, the -- the suggestion that the time issues will in some manner resolve themselves because the accused have the right in due course to testify in their own defence. Your Honour, of course there have been some differences between the Bench and the bar as to the merits of adversarial versus inquisitorial proceedings but these are essentially adversarial proceedings at least to this extent: That the Prosecution bears the burden the of proof, and part of that burden of proof is that by the time the Prosecution closes its case, there must be at least a prima facie case against the accused. Failing that, of course, the Defence can make a motion under 98 bis for a judgement of acquittal. And the concern we have, Your Honour, when the Judges say the accused can testify, that's an issue that should not strictly arise unless and until the Judges have found that there is a case for them to answer. And if the Trial Chamber should have reached a conclusion on that issue before the end of the Prosecution case, obviously that would be a matter of the gravest concern to the Defence, because it would appear that that issue has already been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. I'm going to stop you there, Mr. Murphy. When I said that I had the impression that there was some misunderstanding, when I said that an accused can testify, it is pursuant to the Rules, and the Rules provide for the fact that on the basis of the examination-in-chief by the Prosecutor an accused can testify if he so desires and presents -- after the Prosecution case, that is. And the accused can testify as a witness. So there was a misunderstanding there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, yes, I do understand that. My point is, Your Honour, of course that unless there is a case for the accused to answer, the question of him testifying would not arise, and the Prosecution has the burden initially of persuading the Trial Chamber that there is a case to answer. We certainly don't make that concession and so the burden still rests on the Prosecution. Your Honour, the -- the point that Mr. Praljak made earlier, we feel, was well taken. This witness illustrates perfectly the point that both the Prosecution and the Defence have been making here. We had a witness whose evidence is really vital to both sides as to the understanding of the events on and around the 9th of May and subsequently in 1993. It was obvious from Mr. Scott's direct examination that he felt he did not have time to develop the evidence as he would have wished. A great deal of the evidence was in a sense taken for granted through leading questions. I don't criticise Mr. Scott for that; he had no alternative. But it makes it difficult for the Defence to adequately challenge an and I think in the case of all the accused except perhaps Mr. Coric's counsel we literally ran out of time in the middle of making make what we thought were interesting and compelling points. Now, Your Honour, we do feel -- we've said this before I don't want to repeat it, especially since it is pending in the Appeals Chamber, but nonetheless there does come a time when the rights of both the Prosecution and the accused are prejudiced by the restrictions on time, and I want to again renew the objection we've made to the conduct basis of the trial and ask that ample time be allowed and that the Judges conduct it in the interests of fairness to both parties rather than the completion strategy. And I -- I think I may have spoken for all my colleagues but I think they will amplify my comments if they wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one point, Mr. Murphy. I would like to thank you for telling us that, but to understand what you're saying most exactly, you said that the witness that was here, that there were certain points that he raised and that the Defence did not have a chance because of the time constraints to cross-examine him on those matters. I think that's what you said. Now, what points would you like to raise? What points were they? Because it seems to me that when he responded to the examination-in-chief and the questions of the Judges he answered most of them. But what are you referring to precisely, and what part would you like to have had the opportunity to question the witness about, which points?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour I can only speak for the Stojic Defence on that with any great precision. I know in our case that we had a number of other documents that we would have wished to put to the witness and I think Ms. Nozica would have preferred to ask a large number of other questions arising from the documents that we did put, to go into detail about them. Now, my -- my colleagues will -- will speak for themselves as to their position, but I had the impression as an experienced advocate that in general the cross-examination was necessarily rushed in order to comply with the time limits, as indeed was the direct examination. And it's our position, Your Honour, that in a case of this magnitude, which is in a sense now the flagship of the Tribunal, if I can put it that way, the emphasis should be on a calm and unhurried exploration of the facts rather than a predetermined timetable in deference to the Security Council. We've been through issues before and I know Your Honours understand them, but I just felt in particular regard to this witness it was time perhaps to make this point again because it did arise, I think, particularly clearly today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could just supplement just -- just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Karnavas. I'll just respond to Mr. Murphy, and then I'll give you the floor. While you were talking Mr. Murphy, I was looking at the documents of the cross-examination of your client, and I looked through the documents when there is a cross-examination, and I've just seen that most of the documents were -- you asked about most of the documents. They were presented to this witness and to another. And if you really had a very essential and important document, I wouldn't have missed that. Rest assured I would have raised it of my own accord. So I take note of what you've said, but I do not see in what way your defence was deprived of any of the things you wanted to do pursuant to documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Let me just at this if I may: Of course when we prepare the cross-examination, we're doing so in the light of the time limits that the Trial Chamber imposes on us so we try to discipline ourselves to restrict the cross-examination in that way. But that raises another question. Your Honour refers to the matter of defendants, the accused working together, and, Your Honour, I think it's been indicated in the course of the trial that we try to do that as much as possible. We make joint filings and we try to agree on the time. But again, Your Honour, the -- if the impression is being given that the six accused are operating as in a sense a team, that is not the right impression because each accused is responsible for his own defence. And while we do try to cooperate as far as possible, we are also working in our own client's best interest, and that from time to time will mean that we cannot necessarily agree with our colleagues as to what should -- how the cross-examination should be conducted. And Your Honour, I'm sure, appreciates that facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be heard just very briefly on the points that you raised, Mr. President. From the Prosecution's standpoint this witness was important, in my opinion, one, they wanted to establish what happened to the gentleman, how he was treated, but also because of his position they wanted him to comment on certain documents, documents which they believe would lead the Trial Chamber into believing that it was the HVO that were the aggressors, particularly as it relates to May 9, 1993, setting up their witnesses to follow. At least from a common -- from a common position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. My colleague wanted to say something but let me say that the fact that the HVO on the 9th of May attacked is something that was noted by the Chamber after following the Naletilic trial. Now, if you want to demonstrate the contrary, you can always do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will have an opportunity to do so through your cross-examination and witnesses. But this is a fact that the Trial Chamber took note of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I understand that Judge Trechsel and you come from a different legal system, and I understand that Judge Trechsel believes that I have to put a case on forward. I do not. I can attack their case. The documents that General Praljak wanted to introduce and what we wanted to develop was for you to have a complete picture. Right now your picture is, at least it may be - I don't know but I suspect - that it was the Croats that attacked on May 9th,end of story. What we're trying to show is that there is a great deal of evidence for months on end that the other side was preparing. The other side was positioning itself. The other side was procuring weapons. The other side is issuing orders, orders that are secret. The other side is planting their own men into the HVO not only to gather information but also in order to gather weapons and to attack. And so it leads us then up to May 9 and that we wanted to do today is demonstrate that May 9th is not an open and shut issue. It is something we believe that if it were -- if the HVO were the initial aggressors, if you want to use that word, it was done so on a pre-emptive basis and under international law that is a form of self-defence that is recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: (redacted) point but with respect to these events. We're trying to help you. That's what we're trying to do. I have full confidence that if you have all of the evidence you will make the right decision. But what I'm saying is, please allow me to give you the full picture. And now we see two questions, two very important questions, one from Judge Trechsel, one from Judge Prandler. Both are saying why are you introducing these documents? Why aren't you following up? Well, the answer is very simple: Time. We don't have the time. If we had the time, we would be able. So this has become an exercise of getting the documents in. If you see my cross-examination, I'm rushed to get the documents in hoping at some later time I'm going to be able write out an argument. I don't think this is quite as persuasive. I'm not being critical I understand you're under a tremendous amount of pressure and I sympathise with that but there are some witnesses that I believe we need to be a little bit more flexible on and you will -- you will see that at least this particular Defence team will not abuse any time issue requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, the only pressure that we do have is to have the truth out. There are no other pressures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me help you out, Mr. President. I would be more than happy this help you out, and I'm trying to do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I be allowed, as Mr. Karnavas has gone into some speculations on what my opinion and attitude to the towards might be. I do not think that there is any difference. There may be in certain cases. I may not be as poker faced, perhaps, as the ideal American Judge would be, who, by the way, would not decide either, but I fully accept that the Defence needs the possibility to cast doubts, to present a different picture of reality. Please do not doubt this. That is very legitimate, and I absolutely accept this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, Judge Trechsel, I don't mean to be making any suggestions, but take -- take General Praljak's presentation. He spent a tremendous amount of hours trying to make it as cogent and as concise as possible, and I think half an hour more is not going to kill us. It's not going to kill the UN bank. We're going to make it up somehow. We see one witness isn't able to attend this week. We're going to make it up. We're going to find ways. But important witnesses, when we say to you, Your Honours, we need an extra 15 minutes or half an hour, we don't say that because we want to take up your time; we say it because we know the case. We know how valuable it is, and if you wish for us to give you the heads up, to give you some -- a predicate as to why we need the additional, and what points we're trying to challenge, we'll be more than happy to and perhaps we have failed in communicating that and maybe in the future we will endeavour to do that, but please understand that we are not trying to waste your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Stewart, but before I do so, I'd just like to say this: Mr. Praljak did do a lot of work, put in a lot of work, and the map is a result of a lot of work on his part, and the part that we Judges looked at and we accorded it an IC number is useful. That's quite obvious. But you ask questions and we ask the witness a question and the witness was very clear. So we weren't able to go beyond that. He said that the movement of units did not come under his job and remit; it was logistics. So there we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, go ahead, and we're going to have the witness shown in after that because the witness will be wondering what's happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I would like to say something very briefly but I wonder if General Praljak could have the opportunity first, Your Honour. I didn't see him there behind. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Honours. Precisely this example as to who attacked whom on the 9th of May in Mostar we have seen the Spanish Battalion's report that says that HVO turned back units, and we heard another report about the Muslim who was watching all that. The Chamber actually made its best decision based on -- at -- on Tuta and Stela but based on documents that were not thoroughly examined, and that judgement was made on the very few documents produced. You have evidence that the brigade from Metkovici crossed over to the other side, but I cannot discuss with this witness how many people were killed in Metkovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do not go into substance, because we are now discussing purely procedural issues. As to substance and merit, you will have ample opportunity to discuss it with other witnesses. And of course the Trial Chamber always has the right to invite its own witnesses. Mr. Stewart first and Mr. Scott later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate being allowed the opportunity, if Mr. Scott doesn't mind at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can interrupt. My apologies to Mr. Stewart. The most pressing point of the matter, there's a number of redactions that have to be made very quickly before we lose control of that. Unfortunately, since we have gone into open session there are a number of things that will end to identify the previous witness. So at this time, and I'm happy to give behalf additional time the Chamber wants to give to Mr. Stewart, but I'm obligated to raise this without further delay. There needs to be a redaction on page 97, line 4; a redaction on page 97, line 9; a redaction on page 99, line 19; and a redaction on page 99, line 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will see, but I don't think that anything identifying of the witness was mentioned. I take note of what you said, and we will investigate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I We certainly ask the Chamber to look at it. In our view at least several of them are a bit -- I'm not going to say -- I'm not going to make the problem worse by pointing them again, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the legal officer will tell us, will give us the transcript presently, and we will look into it. Believe me, I was extremely alert on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I give the floor back to Mr. Stewart, but I mean frankly, to be perfectly honest, we're not going to start the witness today which is unfortunate, but I do want to be heard in response. It's not fair to give the Defence collectively 20 or 25 minutes and not give the Prosecution any time to reply. I do want to be heard today after Mr. Stewart has finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll be as quick as I can to -- Mr. Scott can have that opportunity, Your Honour. I don't have very much to say. First of all, our colleagues do speak for the Petkovic Defence on these points as well today. We support and associate ourselves with what they've said. May we just add that Mr. Murphy is completely right to indicate that coordination among the Defence teams, two counsel and a client on every Defence team as a minimum has its distinct limitations as a practical matter. There is only so much we can agree. There is only so much we can do but we assure Your Honour that we do try very hard. And all I have to add to our learned colleagues' submissions is this, Your Honour, that a useful cross-check is a scrutiny of the transcripts of today's hearing and that demonstrates if one looks at the transcripts it demonstrates the pressures on experienced counsel my own lead counsel, for example, in showing documents to the witness was continually in the position where the time pressures prevented her from doing what she clearly wished to do, which was to have the witness scrutinise the document in more detail to answer the questions. The same applied in relation to maps for General Praljak. If these jobs are going to be done and when the work has been done, the preparation has been done, time to actually have the witness look at the material and answer the questions thoroughly is absolutely critical and that cross-check against today's transcript will amply demonstrate the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott. You wanted to say something. You have the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, first of all, I -- just a lead-in to my additional comments. I think it's unfortunate in the last half hour at various times a number of people have started arguing the merits of the case and arguing their positions, and that's not what we're here to do. I could respond to every point that's been made about the Prosecution position, the Prosecution theory of the case, what we contend the evidence shows, but I don't think we should do that now. And I don't think Mr. Praljak should, I don't think other counsel should stand up and again -- arguing the merits of their case. This is a procedural point that's being addressed now, and I appreciate the reason for -- Mr. Murphy's raised it. Now, having said that, Your Honour, I feel the need under these situations, because the Defence comes up and states these positions, and I give them credit to the extent that they've mentioned that some of this applies to the Prosecution as well, but nonetheless I must put a line under that. As Mr. Murphy himself said several times, it is the Prosecution itself in this case that has the burden of proof. The Defence has the burden to prove nothing. And I can assure the Chamber that if anyone in this courtroom feels the constant pressure of time, feels the constant pressures of the limitations that, with all respect, the Chamber has put on the Prosecution case, if anyone feels that most in the courtroom it is the Prosecution. And I cannot -- I simply -- and I also want to say, you know, everyone stands up and says, Your Honour, we worked so hard to present our case and we've put so much effort into that, well, Your Honour, that goes for the Defence -- Prosecution ten times as well. We work very hard. We work weekends, we work at night, we stay all night, we work very hard to present this case to the Chamber the best we can. So I accept what counsel says, but what's -- it's a two-sided coin, Your Honour. Prosecution works very, very hard to try to present this case to the Judges as best we can. We don't do it perfectly; we make mistakes. But if anyone wants to say, Oh, you know, we're so sorry, you know, you're not receiving this, we worked so hard on it, Your Honour the Prosecution works hard on this all the time - all the time - and our ox's doors, so to speak, just like anyone else's or more so. Now, in the circumstances we are in and the reason I made the point yesterday about the allocation of the additional, and I'm going to use the term, "special time," given to each accused when that accused is particularly affected particular evidence. The reason I made that, Your Honour, and I -- I will have to say -- I will say -- I'll slow down. I will say that to take some of these positions is not the position I would like to take. But again, when the Prosecution has been constantly put in this situation and we're put at a disadvantage, when an hour of direct examination is cut, then I have no other alternative; I have no alternative. I am obligated out of fairness to my part of the case to make sure the Chamber understands there is -- the Prosecution is not put at any further disadvantage and indeed, with all respect, that the Defence is not given more favourable treatment or given more time because that time ultimately comes out of the Prosecution case. That is the reality. And then with all respect, that is one of the things led the Chamber to issue its ruling before about cutting the Prosecution time. The Chamber became concerned, I'm sure, with the passage of time on the calendar and therefore in response to that cut the Prosecution's time, and just as the Defence continues to take more time now with all -- and again, I wish we all had more time, but we don't. And with -- our time is limited and the Defence takes more time, at the end of the day, with all respect, the Chamber's going to come back and say, We're going to have to cut the time again because the calendar's going too slow. So it does affect the Prosecution. It affects us directly and importantly. So I -- I'll sit down, Your Honour. I just simply want to make the point for the record, when the Defence stand up and with great respect to Defence counsel who I do have great respect for, they may not think that but I do, but when they stand up and talk about their concerns and how their treatment how their treatment -- how their treatment about getting a fair trial, Your Honour, take what they say and multiply that five times for the Prosecution because we're very concerned about getting a fair trial. And we can't have one side advantaged over the disadvantage of the other. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. We've heard Mr. Scott, and as usual the Judges work together and we're going to deliberate on what both sides said. In any case, I thank you for your remarks. Concerning tomorrow's hearing, as you know, protective measures are envisaged and granted for the witness who I will not name for obvious reasons. They include a pseudonym and facial distortion. Concerning time, we decided a moment ago that inasmuch as we have four hours at our disposal tomorrow, we will give the Prosecution two hours and two hours to the Defence. We would appreciate it very much if nobody went beyond their time limit, and the present arrangements do not envisage and do not make provision for any questions by the Judges or any procedural problems. So please try to stay within your two hours. The next witness, whom I am not naming, will speak to events that have been the subject of testimony by other witnesses. So, Mr. Scott, you can also have two hours for your examination-in-chief. I have to stop here because another trial is schedule for the afternoon, and one of our colleagues is working 10 hours a day at two trials. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 18th day of January, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
